sentence: QT-interval prolongation interactions occur when multiple agents with intrinsic QT-prolonging activity are co-administered. Combinations of antiarrhythmics, certain antipsychotics, fluoroquinolones, methadone, and antifungal azoles can produce additive prolongation with risk of torsades de pointes, particularly in patients with electrolyte disturbance, female sex, advanced age, structural heart disease, or congenital long-QT syndrome. Periodic monitoring of the corrected QT interval with high-risk combinations and avoidance of multiple culprits where possible is the principal preventive measure. Concurrent hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia from diuretic use compound the risk substantially.

Felbamate, although effective in refractory epilepsy and once used as a first-line agent, is now restricted because of idiosyncratic risks of aplastic anaemia at approximately one per four thousand and hepatic failure at approximately one per twenty thousand. The agent is reserved for selected patients in whom alternatives have failed and after detailed informed consent. The case illustrates that even agents with substantial benefit in resistant populations may have a risk profile that makes routine use untenable, and that careful selection of patients with the most to gain is the principal mitigation strategy.

Many drugs and their active metabolites are cleared by the kidney, and when renal function declines without a corresponding reduction in dose, the drug accumulates to toxic concentrations. Gabapentin and pregabalin, both renally eliminated, can produce profound sedation, confusion, and myoclonus in patients with unrecognised renal impairment receiving standard doses, a common and avoidable adverse event.

Drug-induced eosinophilic pneumonia, associated with agents such as daptomycin, certain non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and minocycline, presents with cough, dyspnoea, peripheral eosinophilia, and pulmonary infiltrates. The condition typically resolves after withdrawal of the offending drug, often with corticosteroid treatment, and recognising the drug aetiology spares the patient an unnecessary infectious workup.

Methylphenidate and other stimulants used in attention deficit disorder elevate blood pressure and heart rate in a dose-dependent manner and may unmask underlying cardiac arrhythmias. Insomnia, appetite suppression, and weight loss are common at therapeutic doses, and growth velocity in paediatric patients should be monitored over years of treatment. Rebound symptoms upon withdrawal can mimic an exacerbation of the underlying condition.

Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors such as acetazolamide and the related effect of topiramate produce a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis through renal bicarbonate wasting, and they also promote hypokalaemia. The acidosis contributes to the paraesthesiae and fatigue patients describe and predisposes to renal stone formation.

Posaconazole and isavuconazole, newer triazoles, share the hepatotoxicity, QT prolongation in the case of posaconazole, and CYP3A4 interactions of the class. Isavuconazole, by contrast, shortens the QT interval slightly, which has positioned it as preferred in patients on multiple QT-prolonging agents. Posaconazole oral suspension absorption is highly variable and food-dependent, with the delayed-release tablet and intravenous formulations producing more predictable exposures. Therapeutic drug monitoring is routine for prophylaxis in haematology populations where breakthrough invasive aspergillosis remains a substantial concern.

Oxybutynin and other antimuscarinic agents for overactive bladder produce the predictable peripheral anticholinergic burden of dry mouth, constipation, and blurred vision, but their central effects are of particular concern in older patients, in whom they can impair cognition and have been associated in cohort studies with an increased long-term risk of dementia. Quaternary or more bladder-selective agents are preferred where the cognitive risk is a concern.

Teriparatide, a recombinant parathyroid hormone analogue that builds bone, carried a boxed warning regarding osteosarcoma based on rodent studies in which the tumour developed at high cumulative doses. This led to a recommended limit on the duration of treatment in humans, although long-term surveillance has not confirmed a clinically meaningful osteosarcoma signal, and the warning was subsequently removed.

Shivering in the recovery period, although often dismissed as trivial, sharply increases oxygen consumption and carbon dioxide production, which can be hazardous in patients with limited cardiac or respiratory reserve. It also intensifies postoperative pain and wound tension. The principal driver is intraoperative hypothermia, and active warming together with pharmacologic measures is used to suppress it.

Accidental awareness during general anaesthesia, in which the patient forms explicit memories of intraoperative events, is rare but can produce lasting psychological harm including post-traumatic stress disorder. Risk is elevated during periods of light anaesthesia such as obstetric and cardiac surgery and at the start and end of the anaesthetic, and the use of neuromuscular blockade compounds the distress by preventing the patient from signalling consciousness.

Systemic corticosteroids produce predictable adverse effects roughly proportional to dose and duration, including hyperglycaemia, hypertension, weight gain with central adiposity, osteoporosis, cataracts, gastric ulceration, immune suppression with predisposition to opportunistic infections, mood disturbance ranging from euphoria to frank psychosis, and adrenal suppression that may require slow tapering on cessation. Avascular necrosis of the femoral head is a particularly feared idiosyncratic complication that may develop after a relatively brief course of high-dose therapy. Bone protection with bisphosphonates is recommended for prolonged courses.

Growth hormone therapy in children with growth hormone deficiency is associated with relatively mild adverse effects including injection-site reactions and benign intracranial hypertension, but in adults with hypopituitarism the dose must be carefully titrated to avoid fluid retention, carpal tunnel syndrome, arthralgia, and worsening of insulin resistance. The historical concern about increased malignancy risk has not been confirmed in long-term registry data, although second tumours in survivors of childhood cancer remain a contraindication. The recombinant preparation eliminated the historical risk of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease.

Pain management in older adults must navigate the substantial harms of both NSAIDs and opioids in this population. NSAIDs increase the risk of gastrointestinal bleeding, renal injury, and cardiovascular events and are generally avoided. Opioids, although not formally contraindicated, carry substantially greater risk of cognitive impairment, falls, and constipation in the elderly. Paracetamol, topical agents, and non-pharmacologic strategies including physical therapy and graded activity should be exhausted before chronic systemic analgesic therapy in older adults, and when systemic opioids are required they should be initiated at lower doses than in younger patients.

Anaphylaxis to neuromuscular blocking agents is a leading cause of perioperative anaphylaxis, and sensitisation can occur through prior exposure or, controversially, through cross-reactive quaternary ammonium groups present in some consumer products such as cough medicines and cosmetics. The reaction can be catastrophic, and identifying the culprit agent through subsequent allergy testing is essential for safe future anaesthesia.

Diffuse alveolar haemorrhage can be precipitated by anticoagulants, certain chemotherapeutic agents, and a small number of other drugs, presenting with haemoptysis, falling haemoglobin, and alveolar infiltrates. It is a medical emergency, and the drug history is a crucial part of the evaluation because withdrawal of the responsible agent is integral to management.

A drug-induced tremor, typically a fine postural tremor, is produced by lithium, valproate, beta-agonists, and several other agents, and it can be functionally disabling even when the underlying treatment is otherwise beneficial. Distinguishing it from essential tremor or an emerging neurological disorder rests on its temporal relationship to the drug and its dose dependence.

Mammalian target of rapamycin inhibitors such as sirolimus and everolimus, used in transplant immunosuppression, produce a distinctive toxicity profile including impaired wound healing, oral ulceration, hyperlipidaemia, proteinuria, and a non-infectious interstitial pneumonitis. Their antiproliferative action, while useful in suppressing rejection and certain malignancies, is also responsible for the dehiscence risk that requires their temporary substitution around surgical procedures.

Antithyroid drugs used for hyperthyroidism, carbimazole and propylthiouracil, can produce agranulocytosis, an idiosyncratic and potentially fatal loss of neutrophils that typically appears within the first months of treatment. Patients are counselled to report fever and sore throat promptly, and propylthiouracil additionally carries a risk of severe hepatotoxicity that has restricted its use largely to the first trimester of pregnancy.

Dupilumab, a dual IL-4 and IL-13 receptor antagonist used in atopic dermatitis, asthma, eosinophilic oesophagitis, and chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps, is associated with conjunctivitis in approximately one in ten patients, often requiring ophthalmologic referral and topical management. Facial erythema and head-and-neck dermatitis with a different distribution from baseline atopic disease may emerge during therapy. Eosinophilia and rare cases of eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis have been observed, particularly in patients tapering oral corticosteroids.

The dopamine agonist withdrawal syndrome, seen in Parkinson disease and restless legs syndrome when these drugs are tapered, produces anxiety, panic, depression, pain, and autonomic symptoms that can be refractory to other treatments. It is the mirror image of the impulse-control disorders the agonists can cause, and it can leave patients unable to discontinue a drug despite a clear indication to do so.

Metronidazole, used for anaerobic infections, amoebiasis, giardiasis, and trichomoniasis, produces a metallic taste, mild gastrointestinal upset, and a well-known disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol that should be disclosed to all patients receiving the drug. Prolonged or high-dose courses produce dose-related peripheral neuropathy that may be only partially reversible after discontinuation, and rarely a cerebellar syndrome with characteristic MRI signal abnormalities in the dentate nuclei. Pseudomembranous colitis from Clostridioides difficile is paradoxically associated with the drug despite being used as a treatment.

Stopping an anticonvulsant abruptly in a patient with epilepsy can precipitate seizures, including status epilepticus, even when the drug was being used for a non-epilepsy indication such as mood stabilisation. Withdrawal seizures are a particular hazard with barbiturates and benzodiazepines, and any planned discontinuation of an antiepileptic drug requires a gradual reduction schedule.

subtopic: gene therapy and viral vector toxicity
sentence: Because integrating and even some non-integrating gene therapies produce a permanent or long-lasting genetic modification, an adverse effect of the therapy cannot be reversed by withdrawing a drug, and there is no analogue of dose cessation. This irreversibility fundamentally changes the risk calculus compared with conventional pharmacotherapy.

The theoretical concern that potent adjuvants might trigger or unmask autoimmune disease has been raised repeatedly, and a contested entity grouping such reactions has been proposed, but large epidemiological studies have not established a consistent causal link for licensed adjuvanted vaccines. The discrepancy between biological plausibility and population-level evidence is itself instructive about how adjuvant safety must be assessed.

Extravasation of iodinated contrast during power injection delivers a hyperosmolar fluid into the subcutaneous tissues, producing pain, swelling, and in severe cases compartment syndrome or skin necrosis requiring surgical intervention. The risk is greatest with high injection rates, small peripheral veins, and patients unable to report pain, and the volume injected before the malfunction is detected determines the severity of the tissue injury.

Intravenous bisphosphonate infusion frequently produces an acute-phase reaction within the first one to three days, with fever, myalgia, arthralgia, and flu-like symptoms, particularly after the first dose. The reaction reflects cytokine release from gamma-delta T cells and tends to diminish with subsequent infusions, but it can be alarming to patients who were not warned to expect it.

Patients with deficient or atypical plasma cholinesterase metabolise succinylcholine slowly, resulting in a prolonged paralysis that may last hours rather than minutes, leaving the patient apnoeic long after the expected duration. The condition, termed suxamethonium apnoea, is genetically determined, and affected individuals require supportive ventilation until the block resolves spontaneously.

Contrast-associated acute kidney injury, although its incidence and causal contribution have been substantially revised downward by studies using contemporary low-osmolar agents and matched control groups, remains a genuine concern in patients with pre-existing severe renal impairment, particularly diabetics. Hydration before and after contrast administration is the principal evidence-supported preventive measure, while the once-routine use of acetylcysteine and bicarbonate has fallen out of favour after large negative trials.

Cyproheptadine, an antihistamine with additional antiserotonergic activity, stimulates appetite and is sometimes used deliberately for that purpose, but the weight gain and sedation are unwanted effects when the drug is used for its antihistaminic indication. Its antiserotonergic action also makes it useful as an antidote in serotonin syndrome, a repurposing of one drug's side-effect profile.

Loop diuretics produce dose-dependent ototoxicity, particularly at the high intravenous doses used in resistant oedema and following rapid infusion. Hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hyperuricaemia precipitating gout, and dehydration with prerenal azotaemia are common. Thiazide diuretics share many of these metabolic effects and additionally raise plasma glucose and worsen control in established diabetes, often becoming clinically apparent at doses above twenty-five milligrams of hydrochlorothiazide daily.

Combining triptans with serotonergic antidepressants raised concern about serotonin syndrome, prompting a regulatory advisory, although subsequent analysis has suggested that the actual risk of clinically significant serotonin toxicity from this specific combination is low. The episode illustrates how a theoretically plausible interaction can generate a warning that exceeds the evidence and complicates the treatment of patients with both migraine and depression.

Drug-induced lupus, provoked by agents such as hydralazine, procainamide, and certain anti-TNF biologics, can include pleuritis and pleural effusion as a prominent respiratory manifestation. The syndrome usually resolves after withdrawal of the offending drug, and recognising the medication trigger distinguishes it from idiopathic systemic lupus erythematosus, which carries a different prognosis and treatment.

Pregnancy increases the requirement for levothyroxine substantially, and failure to increase the dose in early gestation leaves the fetus exposed to maternal hypothyroidism at a critical period of neurodevelopment. The adverse outcome here arises not from the drug but from underreplacement, illustrating that inadequate dosing is itself a form of treatment-related harm.

Benzodiazepines and other sedatives occasionally produce paradoxical agitation, disinhibition, and aggression rather than the expected calming effect, an outcome more common in children, in the elderly, and in patients with certain personality traits. The reaction can lead to escalating doses if it is misread as inadequate sedation, worsening the disinhibition further.

Aminoglycoside antibiotics, magnesium, and certain other drugs potentiate neuromuscular blockade by interfering with acetylcholine release or postsynaptic function, and their administration in the perioperative period can prolong paralysis or recurarise a patient who appeared to have recovered. This interaction is particularly important in obstetric patients receiving magnesium for pre-eclampsia who then require anaesthesia.

Benzodiazepine withdrawal after prolonged use can produce a protracted syndrome of anxiety, insomnia, perceptual disturbance, and, in severe cases, seizures and a delirium resembling that of alcohol withdrawal. The risk is greatest with high doses and short-half-life agents, and a slow, individualised taper, sometimes over many months, is required to avoid these potentially dangerous discontinuation effects.

Photodynamic therapy with topical aminolevulinic acid produces predictable but often severe stinging and burning during light exposure and a sunburn-like reaction over the following days that requires strict photoprotection. The therapy is otherwise well tolerated. Topical 5-fluorouracil applied to actinic keratoses produces erythema, crusting, and erosion that may be cosmetically distressing during the treatment course; patients commonly require detailed counselling about the expected severity, and discontinuation due to local toxicity is the most common reason for incomplete therapy.

Long-term suppression of bone remodelling by antiresorptive drugs may, paradoxically, impair the repair of microdamage that accumulates in bone during normal loading, and this is the proposed mechanism for atypical femoral fractures, which characteristically begin in the lateral cortex and may be preceded by prodromal thigh pain. Periodic reassessment of the need for continued therapy, sometimes termed a drug holiday, addresses this concern.

Topical anaesthetics such as proparacaine and tetracaine, although essential for clinical procedures, are toxic to the corneal epithelium with repeated use and cause delayed re-epithelialisation, persistent epithelial defects, and microbial keratitis. The phenomenon of topical-anaesthetic abuse keratopathy, occasionally seen in patients who obtain these agents for self-treatment of ocular pain, can rapidly progress to stromal melting and corneal perforation requiring transplantation. Patient education on the toxicity of chronic use is critical when supplies are dispensed.

Delayed haemolytic transfusion reactions occur days to weeks after transfusion when an anamnestic antibody response to a minor red cell antigen develops, producing a falling haemoglobin and jaundice that may be mistaken for bleeding or another cause of anaemia. The delayed timing obscures the link to the earlier transfusion.

Trastuzumab, although better tolerated than anthracyclines, produces a reversible decline in left ventricular ejection fraction in approximately five percent of treated patients, with substantially higher rates when combined with anthracyclines concurrently. Baseline and serial echocardiography or radionuclide ventriculography are required, and treatment is generally interrupted for asymptomatic ejection fraction declines below institutional thresholds.

Fluoroquinolones were historically avoided in children because of cartilage damage observed in juvenile animal studies. Subsequent clinical experience suggests that arthropathy in treated children is reversible and uncommon, and the agents are now used selectively for serious infections including complicated urinary tract infection, pseudomonal infection, and as part of multidrug regimens for resistant tuberculosis. The risk-benefit balance in children must weigh the species-specific cartilage findings against the alternatives, which may be parenteral and toxic or include the use of even more restricted second-line agents.

Protamine sulfate reverses unfractionated heparin but is itself associated with significant adverse effects. Rapid intravenous administration produces hypotension and bradycardia through histamine release, and a catastrophic pulmonary vasoconstriction with right heart failure has been described, particularly in patients previously sensitised through protamine-containing insulin or prior cardiac surgery. Paradoxically, excess protamine has a mild intrinsic anticoagulant effect, so overcorrection can worsen rather than control bleeding.

High-dose vitamin K given to reverse warfarin overanticoagulation produces a period of warfarin resistance lasting one to two weeks, during which re-establishing therapeutic anticoagulation is difficult and patients with mechanical heart valves are exposed to thromboembolic risk. Intravenous administration carries a small risk of anaphylactoid reaction, and oral and subcutaneous routes have unpredictable absorption that may delay correction in urgent situations.

Andexanet alfa reverses apixaban and rivaroxaban by acting as a decoy factor Xa, but its use has been complicated by thrombotic events in roughly one in ten treated patients and by a rebound rise in anti-Xa activity after the infusion ends. The drug also interferes with heparin assays, confounding subsequent monitoring if heparin anticoagulation is restarted, and its high cost relative to prothrombin complex concentrate remains a barrier to routine use.

Aminoglycosides such as gentamicin and amikacin produce dose- and duration-dependent nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity. The vestibular component of ototoxicity tends to be irreversible and can present long after the antibiotic course has concluded. Once-daily extended-interval dosing achieves equivalent bactericidal effect with somewhat lower toxicity by exploiting the post-antibiotic effect, and trough monitoring remains essential to confirm clearance between doses.

Topical retinoids including tretinoin and adapalene routinely produce initial irritation, erythema, peeling, and a transient acneiform flare during the first weeks of therapy, often misinterpreted by patients as treatment failure. Photosensitivity is increased and rigorous sun protection is essential. Oral isotretinoin produces a substantially more severe constellation including cheilitis, mucocutaneous dryness, hypertriglyceridaemia, transaminase elevation, and a small but well-documented signal for mood disturbance that warrants careful screening and disclosure.

Excessive levothyroxine in childhood can advance bone maturation and, through premature closure of the growth plates, compromise final adult height, while underreplacement impairs growth and neurodevelopment. The narrow target range for thyroid hormone in paediatric replacement reflects this dual hazard at both ends of the dosing spectrum.

Loperamide, a peripheral opioid agonist used for diarrhoea, was historically considered devoid of central nervous system effects because of poor blood-brain barrier penetration. However, high-dose misuse, sometimes promoted in online forums for opioid effect or for management of opioid withdrawal, has produced fatal QT prolongation and torsades de pointes through inhibition of cardiac potassium channels. Regulatory responses have included packaging restrictions and warnings, and clinicians should consider intentional overdose in patients presenting with otherwise unexplained ventricular arrhythmias.

A characteristic feature of some hepatotoxic reactions is hepatic adaptation, in which mild aminotransferase elevations that appear early in treatment resolve despite continued exposure, as seen historically with certain antituberculous and statin therapy. Distinguishing this benign adaptation from the early stage of a progressive injury is a central clinical judgement in monitoring liver chemistry during drug treatment.

Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors typically cause nausea, diarrhoea, headache, and insomnia during the first weeks of therapy, with most symptoms attenuating after the first month. Sexual dysfunction including delayed orgasm and reduced libido is common, occurs in up to half of patients, and does not consistently resolve with continued use. SIADH and bleeding risk, particularly when combined with NSAIDs, warrant attention in older patients.

Class III antiarrhythmics such as sotalol and dofetilide prolong the QT interval as their intended therapeutic mechanism, which makes them inherently proarrhythmic, and the initiation of dofetilide is therefore conventionally performed during an inpatient monitoring period. The therapeutic paradox is stark: the drug that controls the arrhythmia carries within the same mechanism the capacity to provoke a fatal one.

Thrombolytic agents used in acute ischaemic stroke and myocardial infarction carry the highest bleeding risk of the antithrombotic drugs, with symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage being the feared complication that can convert a treatable event into a fatal one. The narrow eligibility criteria for thrombolysis exist largely to identify patients in whom this bleeding risk is acceptable.

Desiccated thyroid extract, derived from animal glands, delivers a fixed and non-physiological ratio of thyroxine to triiodothyronine, and the relatively high triiodothyronine content can produce symptomatic peaks after dosing. Batch-to-batch variability in hormone content has also been documented, introducing an unpredictability into replacement that the synthetic preparations were designed to eliminate.

Repeated red cell transfusion in chronically transfused patients, such as those with thalassaemia or myelodysplasia, leads to iron overload, since the body has no efficient route to excrete the iron delivered with each unit. The accumulated iron deposits in the heart, liver, and endocrine glands, producing cardiomyopathy and organ failure, and necessitates lifelong iron chelation therapy.

The cumulative immunosuppression required to prevent graft rejection markedly increases the long-term risk of malignancy, with non-melanoma skin cancers, post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder driven by Epstein-Barr virus, and several virally mediated cancers occurring at sharply elevated rates. This iatrogenic cancer burden is a defining late complication of transplantation and necessitates lifelong dermatologic and oncologic surveillance.

Nebulised hypertonic saline, used to improve mucus clearance in cystic fibrosis and bronchiectasis, frequently provokes cough and transient bronchoconstriction, necessitating pretreatment with a bronchodilator. The osmotic stimulus that thins secretions is the same property that irritates hyperreactive airways, and a minority of patients cannot tolerate the therapy despite this premedication strategy.

Iodinated contrast can precipitate thyrotoxicosis in patients with autonomous thyroid nodules or latent Graves disease through the iodine load, a phenomenon termed the Jod-Basedow effect, which may emerge weeks after the imaging study. Conversely, in susceptible patients the iodine excess can induce hypothyroidism. These delayed thyroid effects are easily missed because the temporal link to a prior contrast study is not obvious to the clinician evaluating the new endocrine abnormality.

Neuromuscular blockade reversal with neostigmine produces cholinergic excess including bradycardia, hypersalivation, bronchospasm, and gastrointestinal hypermotility, which requires concurrent administration of an anticholinergic agent such as glycopyrrolate. The newer reversal agent sugammadex, a cyclodextrin that encapsulates rocuronium and vecuronium directly, has largely supplanted neostigmine in many practices and carries a much cleaner adverse effect profile, though anaphylaxis at a small but recognised rate and interactions with hormonal contraceptives requiring backup contraception for one week are important clinical considerations.

Medication-overuse headache is a paradoxical adverse effect in which frequent use of acute migraine treatments, including triptans, opioids, and simple analgesics, transforms an episodic headache disorder into a chronic daily headache. The condition only resolves on withdrawal of the overused medication, a process that itself produces a transient worsening of headache and is a recognised barrier to recovery.

Vaginal oestrogen preparations used in postmenopausal genitourinary syndrome produce systemic absorption that is generally clinically insignificant, with serum oestradiol levels remaining largely within the postmenopausal range. The package insert class warnings derived from systemic HRT studies overstate the risks in this local application context. Breast cancer survivors may use these preparations under specialist guidance when non-hormonal alternatives are inadequate, with the caveat that aromatase inhibitor users should generally avoid them because of the theoretical concern about further reducing systemic oestrogen suppression.

Specific HLA alleles predispose to idiosyncratic liver injury from particular drugs, and the association between the HLA-B*5701 allele and flucloxacillin cholestatic hepatitis is a well-characterised example. These genetic associations help explain the host-dependent unpredictability of idiosyncratic injury and raise the prospect of targeted pharmacogenomic screening for selected high-risk drug and population combinations.

The intranasal live attenuated influenza vaccine has been associated with mild upper respiratory symptoms including rhinorrhoea and nasal congestion in the days following administration. It is contraindicated in immunocompromised patients, in pregnancy, and in children under two given a small increased risk of wheezing. Inactivated injectable formulations are preferred in these populations and produce predominantly local injection-site reactions.

subtopic: wound care and topical antiseptic toxicity
sentence: Povidone-iodine applied to large wounds or body cavities can deliver enough absorbed iodine to disturb thyroid function, producing either iodine-induced hypothyroidism or thyrotoxicosis, and to cause metabolic acidosis and renal impairment in extreme cases. Neonates are particularly vulnerable, and excessive cutaneous iodine exposure in the newborn has produced transient hypothyroidism detectable on screening.

Idarucizumab rapidly neutralises dabigatran in life-threatening haemorrhage, but reversal restores the prothrombotic state that originally indicated anticoagulation, and thrombotic events have been observed within days of administration when therapeutic anticoagulation is not promptly reinstated. A small fraction of patients show recurrence of measurable dabigatran activity hours after a single dose, attributed to redistribution of drug from peripheral tissues, occasionally requiring a second dose. Hypersensitivity reactions to the humanised antibody fragment have been reported.

The copper intrauterine device, although hormonally inert, produces increased menstrual bleeding and dysmenorrhoea, particularly in the first months after insertion, with up to ten percent of users requesting removal within the first year for this reason. Uterine perforation at insertion is uncommon at approximately one per thousand and increases during the postpartum and lactation period. Pelvic inflammatory disease risk is concentrated in the first three weeks after insertion in patients with pre-existing untreated genital infection, after which the risk falls to background.

Bodybuilding and weight-loss supplements adulterated with undeclared pharmaceutical agents, including selective androgen receptor modulators, sibutramine analogues, and stimulants, have produced hepatotoxicity, cardiovascular events, and psychiatric disturbance in users who believed they were taking benign natural products. Because the harmful constituent is hidden, clinicians evaluating these presentations may not initially suspect a drug effect, delaying recognition and reporting.

Atovaquone-proguanil for malaria prophylaxis is generally well tolerated, with gastrointestinal upset, vivid dreams, and headache as the dominant complaints. The agent must be taken with fatty food for adequate absorption, a requirement that complicates compliance in some travellers. Atovaquone is also used in Pneumocystis jiroveci prophylaxis in patients intolerant of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, and in toxoplasmosis. Rifampicin, rifabutin, and tetracyclines reduce atovaquone exposures sufficiently to warrant avoidance of these combinations.

Finasteride and dutasteride, 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors used for benign prostatic enlargement and male pattern hair loss, can cause decreased libido, erectile dysfunction, and ejaculatory disturbance. A subset of users report persistent sexual and mood symptoms continuing after the drug is discontinued, a contested entity termed post-finasteride syndrome. The drugs also halve serum prostate-specific antigen, a change that must be accounted for to avoid masking prostate cancer during screening.

Phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors used for erectile dysfunction produce headache, flushing, nasal congestion, and visual disturbances, and their concurrent use with nitrates is absolutely contraindicated because the combined vasodilation can produce profound, refractory hypotension. Rare reports of non-arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy and sudden sensorineural hearing loss have prompted label warnings, although a definitive causal relationship remains difficult to establish.

Sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors confer cardiovascular and renal benefits but introduce specific adverse effects, including a substantial increase in mycotic genital infections and a smaller but consistent increase in urinary tract infections. Euglycaemic diabetic ketoacidosis is a recognised hazard, particularly in the setting of acute illness, fasting, or low-carbohydrate intake, and presents with relatively modest glucose elevations that may delay diagnosis.

Drug-induced pulmonary hypertension is a recognised entity, with the appetite suppressants fenfluramine and aminorex providing the historical paradigm after they produced clusters of a disease previously considered rare. More recently certain tyrosine kinase inhibitors have been implicated, and the latency between exposure and clinical presentation often obscures the causal link.

Topical corticosteroids of high potency such as clobetasol propionate produce dose- and duration-dependent skin atrophy, telangiectasia, striae, and steroid acne or rosacea with prolonged or inappropriate use. Periocular and intertriginous application carries a particular risk. Topical steroid withdrawal syndrome, with rebound erythema and burning on cessation after prolonged use of high-potency agents on facial or genital skin, has gained recognition in dermatologic and patient communities and complicates the management of chronic dermatoses where the drug has been used inappropriately.

Allergic transfusion reactions, ranging from urticaria to anaphylaxis, are caused by recipient antibodies against donor plasma proteins, and severe anaphylactic reactions have occurred in IgA-deficient recipients who have formed anti-IgA antibodies. For such patients, washed cellular components or products from IgA-deficient donors are required to avoid recurrence.

Spinal and epidural haematoma is a rare but devastating complication of neuraxial anaesthesia performed in a patient receiving antithrombotic therapy, and it can produce permanent paraplegia if not decompressed promptly. Detailed guidelines specify the intervals that must elapse between an antithrombotic dose and the placement or removal of a neuraxial catheter.

Opioids used chronically suppress the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, producing a clinically significant hypogonadism with reduced libido, infertility, fatigue, and loss of bone density in both men and women. This opioid-induced endocrinopathy is frequently undiagnosed because its symptoms are attributed to the underlying pain condition rather than to the analgesic itself.

Reactogenicity from adjuvanted vaccines tends to be more pronounced after subsequent doses in a series, as the primed immune system mounts a brisker response to the adjuvant and antigen together. This dose-dependent escalation of fever and malaise is predictable and is a recognised reason for incomplete vaccine series when recipients are not counselled to expect it.

Nitrofurantoin can produce both an acute pulmonary reaction, with fever, cough, and eosinophilia appearing within days of exposure, and a chronic interstitial fibrosis that develops insidiously over months to years of continuous prophylactic use. The chronic form is particularly important because long-term low-dose nitrofurantoin is widely prescribed for recurrent urinary infection, often without periodic reassessment.

Sinusoidal obstruction syndrome and nodular regenerative hyperplasia represent vascular patterns of drug-induced liver injury, distinct from the hepatocellular and cholestatic categories, and are produced by agents including oxaliplatin, certain thiopurines, and high-dose conditioning chemotherapy. They illustrate that drug toxicity can target the hepatic vasculature and sinusoidal endothelium rather than the hepatocyte itself.

Renal function declines with age, and creatinine-based estimates of glomerular filtration may overestimate true renal function in patients with low muscle mass. Medications eliminated predominantly by the kidney, including direct-acting oral anticoagulants, gabapentin, allopurinol, and several antibiotics, may accumulate to toxic concentrations when dosed on assumed normal renal function. Cystatin C-based estimates of GFR can provide a complementary measure where clinical suspicion of overestimation is high. The combination of polypharmacy with renal dose-adjusted medications is a major source of preventable hospitalisations.

Amiodarone disrupts thyroid function through several mechanisms, its high iodine content and its direct effects on the gland and on thyroid hormone metabolism producing either hypothyroidism or one of two distinct forms of thyrotoxicosis. The distinction between the two thyrotoxic types matters because their treatments diverge, and the disruption can be difficult to resolve given the drug's persistence in tissues.

Dry powder inhalers require an adequate inspiratory flow to disaggregate and deliver the medication, and patients with severe airflow limitation or acute exacerbation may generate insufficient flow, resulting in poor lung deposition and an apparent loss of therapeutic effect. The mismatch between device and patient capability is a recognised cause of treatment failure that is not a property of the drug itself but of the delivery system.

Postoperative urinary retention, particularly after spinal anaesthesia and in patients receiving opioids or anticholinergic agents, can produce bladder overdistension with lasting detrusor dysfunction if not detected and relieved. Bladder ultrasound surveillance in the recovery area allows timely catheterisation, and the complication is one of several reasons for caution with neuraxial anaesthesia in patients with pre-existing voiding difficulty.

subtopic: wound care and topical antiseptic toxicity
sentence: Hydrogen peroxide and other cytotoxic antiseptics, although effective against microbes, also damage fibroblasts and keratinocytes and can impair the granulation and epithelialisation needed for wound healing. This recognition has shifted wound care away from routine use of cytotoxic agents in clean granulating wounds, reserving them for specific situations of heavy contamination.

Ivermectin used in onchocerciasis, strongyloidiasis, and scabies is generally extremely well tolerated. The Mazzotti reaction, an inflammatory response to dying microfilariae in onchocerciasis with rash, lymphadenopathy, and ocular inflammation, can be severe and is partly attributable to the parasitic burden rather than to the drug itself. Coinfection with Loa loa contraindicates ivermectin in some endemic regions because severe encephalopathy may follow microfilarial killing. The agent has been investigated and rejected as a COVID-19 treatment, though it has retained substantial off-label use against the recommendation of regulatory bodies.

Buprenorphine, a partial mu-opioid agonist used in maintenance treatment, can precipitate an acute withdrawal syndrome if administered while a full agonist still occupies the receptors, because its high affinity displaces the full agonist while delivering less intrinsic activity. Induction timing must therefore be carefully managed, and precipitated withdrawal is a recognised and distressing complication of inappropriately early dosing.

Contrast-induced nephropathy, aminoglycoside toxicity, and other nephrotoxic exposures can themselves cause the renal impairment that then leads to accumulation of co-administered drugs, creating a cascade in which one nephrotoxic event amplifies the toxicity of an entire regimen. Recognising this self-reinforcing loop is essential in the management of the acutely unwell, polypharmacy patient.

Anti-TNF biologics including infliximab, etanercept, and adalimumab predispose to reactivation of latent tuberculosis, fungal infections, and hepatitis B, mandating screening with interferon-gamma release assay, hepatitis serology, and chest imaging prior to initiation. Demyelinating disease may emerge or worsen on therapy, and a small increased risk of lymphoma is recognised, particularly hepatosplenic T-cell lymphoma in young men receiving combined immunosuppression for inflammatory bowel disease.

Febrile non-haemolytic transfusion reactions, the most common adverse reaction to transfusion, result from recipient antibodies against donor leucocytes or from accumulated cytokines in stored components. Although usually benign, the fever must be distinguished from the early presentation of a haemolytic or septic reaction, and prestorage leucoreduction has reduced its frequency.

Spironolactone, while protective in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, produces hyperkalaemia particularly in patients with reduced renal function or concurrent ACE inhibitor or ARB therapy. Gynaecomastia, breast tenderness, and menstrual irregularities arise from antiandrogenic and progestogenic activity at the steroid receptors. The selective mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist eplerenone has a substantially lower incidence of these endocrine effects.

St John's wort is a potent inducer of cytochrome P450 3A4 and intestinal P-glycoprotein, and its concurrent use reduces plasma concentrations of a wide range of drugs including ciclosporin, oral contraceptives, certain antiretrovirals, and direct oral anticoagulants. Documented consequences include transplant rejection, contraceptive failure with unintended pregnancy, and loss of virological control, making it one of the most clinically significant herb-drug interactions yet characterised.

Barium sulfate suspensions used for gastrointestinal imaging are inert when confined to the bowel lumen, but leakage through an unsuspected perforation into the peritoneal cavity produces a severe granulomatous peritonitis with high mortality. Where perforation is suspected, water-soluble iodinated contrast is substituted, although aspiration of hyperosmolar water-soluble agents into the lung carries its own hazard of pulmonary oedema.

Desmopressin used in nocturnal enuresis and central diabetes insipidus produces hyponatraemia particularly in older patients and with concomitant fluid loading. Severe hyponatraemia with seizure and coma may result from concurrent thiazide diuretic use or excessive water intake. Restrictions on the dosing in older patients and a requirement to limit fluid intake in the hours after each dose have reduced but not eliminated this complication. Headache is the most common minor adverse effect.

Vesicular monoamine transporter inhibitors developed to treat tardive dyskinesia themselves carry a risk of inducing parkinsonism and depression, the latter a notable concern given the historical association of the related drug reserpine with depressed mood. The treatment of one drug-induced movement disorder thus carries the potential to provoke another.

Ibuprofen has produced a small but reproducible association with aseptic meningitis, particularly in patients with underlying systemic lupus erythematosus or other connective tissue disease, mediated through hypersensitivity rather than dose-dependent toxicity. The reaction recurs reliably on rechallenge and constitutes a contraindication to all NSAIDs in affected individuals. Other idiosyncratic NSAID reactions include nephritis, hepatitis, and toxic epidermal necrolysis, the latter particularly with oxicams and some pyrazolone derivatives now largely withdrawn.

Dexmedetomidine, a selective alpha-2 agonist used for procedural sedation and in intensive care, produces dose-dependent bradycardia and hypotension that may be profound in volume-depleted or beta-blocked patients. Rebound hypertension and tachycardia on abrupt discontinuation after prolonged infusion is recognised, paralleling the experience with clonidine. The drug has the unusual property of producing arousable sedation that resembles non-REM sleep, with reduced delirium incidence compared with benzodiazepines in critically ill patients, which has driven its widespread adoption despite the cardiovascular burden.

Albendazole, used in a broad range of helminth infections, produces dose-related transaminitis with prolonged courses for echinococcosis and a relatively rare bone marrow suppression with neutropenia. Mebendazole shares the gastrointestinal upset and rare neutropenia but is less effective in tissue-stage parasites. Both drugs are teratogenic and contraindicated in pregnancy, although inadvertent first-trimester exposure has not produced clearly elevated malformation rates in observational data, providing some reassurance for the not uncommon clinical scenario of treatment of helminthiasis discovered later to have occurred in early pregnancy.

Delayed awakening from anaesthesia prompts a structured search for causes including residual anaesthetic and sedative effect, opioid overdose, hypoglycaemia, hypothermia, electrolyte disturbance, and, most seriously, an intraoperative cerebrovascular event. The recovery-room clinician must distinguish a pharmacologically prolonged but benign emergence from a structural neurological catastrophe, because the management and prognosis diverge completely.

Cannabidiol, approved for Dravet and Lennox-Gastaut syndromes and tuberous sclerosis-associated seizures, produces hepatotoxicity in a dose-related manner particularly in combination with valproate or clobazam. Transaminitis is common and severe injury occasional, requiring monitoring of liver function and adjustment of co-medications. Diarrhoea, decreased appetite, and somnolence are also common. The agent is a potent CYP enzyme inhibitor and interacts with clobazam to elevate the active metabolite N-desmethylclobazam several fold, requiring downward titration of clobazam in many patients.

Several chemotherapeutic and targeted agents can cause drug-induced interstitial lung disease, and the mTOR inhibitors, certain tyrosine kinase inhibitors, and immune checkpoint inhibitor-related pneumonitis have added new entities to this list. Pneumonitis from checkpoint inhibitors in particular requires high-dose immunosuppression and can be fatal if not recognised early.

Halothane, a volatile anaesthetic now largely abandoned in many countries, was associated with a rare but often fatal immune-mediated hepatitis, particularly after repeated exposures, in which trifluoroacetylated liver proteins became the target of an antibody response. The recognition of halothane hepatitis was a major influence on the development of less hepatotoxic successor agents.

Echinocandins including caspofungin, micafungin, and anidulafungin are generally well tolerated, with histamine-mediated infusion reactions, transaminitis, and rare hepatotoxicity the principal concerns. The class targets fungal cell wall beta-1,3-glucan synthase, with no human homologue, accounting for the favourable safety profile. Resistance has emerged particularly in Candida glabrata and is increasingly clinically important. Drug interactions are fewer than with the azoles, with caspofungin metabolism affected by rifampicin, dexamethasone, and selected anticonvulsants requiring dose adjustment.

Mycophenolate mofetil, a mainstay of maintenance immunosuppression after solid organ transplantation, commonly produces gastrointestinal toxicity with diarrhoea, abdominal cramping, and a colitis that can histologically mimic graft-versus-host disease or inflammatory bowel disease. Dose-related leucopenia and anaemia require regular blood count monitoring, and the drug is strongly teratogenic, mandating effective contraception and pregnancy prevention counselling in recipients of childbearing potential.

Immune checkpoint inhibitors targeting PD-1, PD-L1, or CTLA-4 produce a distinctive spectrum of immune-related adverse events including colitis, hepatitis, pneumonitis, hypophysitis, thyroiditis, and a small but persistent risk of fulminant type 1 diabetes. Onset may occur weeks to months after the last dose, and management typically requires high-dose corticosteroids and, in refractory cases, second-line immunosuppression. CTLA-4 blockade is associated with higher toxicity rates than PD-1 monotherapy.

Cytomegalovirus is the most clinically important opportunistic infection in transplant recipients, and the intensity of immunosuppression determines the risk of viral reactivation or primary infection, which can manifest as pneumonitis, colitis, retinitis, or a marrow-suppressing syndrome. Prophylactic or pre-emptive antiviral strategies are standard, but the antivirals themselves, particularly ganciclovir and valganciclovir, add their own burden of neutropenia.

Topical minoxidil for androgenetic alopecia, although well tolerated in most users, produces dose-related hypertrichosis in non-target areas through accidental transfer or systemic absorption, with periorbital and facial hair growth a common patient concern. Initial telogen effluvium and a transient apparent worsening of hair loss often occur during the first two months. Oral low-dose minoxidil has gained increasing use off-label, with attendant cardiovascular adverse effects including peripheral oedema, pericardial effusion in rare cases, and reflex tachycardia.

Massive transfusion produces metabolic derangements including citrate toxicity with hypocalcaemia, since the anticoagulant citrate in stored blood chelates the recipient's calcium, as well as hyperkalaemia from potassium leaked from stored red cells, hypothermia from rapidly infused cold blood, and a dilutional coagulopathy. These cumulative effects require active monitoring and correction during large-volume resuscitation.

Inhaled antibiotics used in cystic fibrosis and non-cystic-fibrosis bronchiectasis, including tobramycin and colistin, can provoke bronchospasm, cough, and an unpleasant taste, and prolonged use selects for resistant organisms within the airway. Systemic absorption is generally low, but measurable serum concentrations may accumulate in patients with renal impairment, raising the theoretical risk of the nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity associated with the intravenous routes.

Four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate, used to reverse warfarin or factor Xa inhibitors, carries a recognised risk of arterial and venous thrombosis because it delivers a concentrated bolus of procoagulant factors into a patient whose underlying condition favours clotting. Disseminated intravascular coagulation and myocardial infarction have followed administration. The heparin contained in some formulations precludes their use in patients with a history of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia.

Transfusion-associated circulatory overload occurs when the volume of transfused blood components exceeds the recipient's cardiovascular capacity, producing acute pulmonary oedema, hypertension, and respiratory distress within hours. It is one of the most common causes of transfusion-related mortality and is particularly hazardous in elderly patients and those with pre-existing cardiac or renal impairment.

Lamotrigine carries a small but established risk of severe cutaneous adverse reactions including Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis, particularly with rapid dose escalation or concomitant valproate, which inhibits its metabolism. Slow titration over six weeks substantially reduces this risk and is mandatory in clinical practice. Any rash within the first eight weeks of treatment warrants prompt clinical assessment.

Opioids and sedatives depress the central respiratory drive, and a drug-induced reduction in ventilation, rather than a structural lung lesion, is the mechanism behind much medication-related respiratory failure. The hazard is amplified by the combination of a sedative with an opioid and by the presence of obstructive sleep apnoea, in which the respiratory consequences are profound.

Inhaled anaesthetics depress myocardial contractility and cause vasodilation, producing a dose-dependent fall in blood pressure, and they also blunt the ventilatory response to carbon dioxide and hypoxia. These cardiovascular and respiratory depressant effects are intrinsic to the agents and require continuous monitoring and support throughout their administration.

Sevoflurane is degraded by the carbon dioxide absorbents in the anaesthetic breathing circuit, particularly when these are desiccated, producing a vinyl ether known as compound A that is nephrotoxic in animal models. Concern about this degradation product shaped recommendations regarding minimum fresh gas flow rates for sevoflurane anaesthesia.

Beta-adrenergic antagonists may precipitate bronchospasm in susceptible patients and are traditionally avoided in asthma, although cardioselective agents at low dose are now used cautiously in some patients with concurrent ischaemic heart disease. Bradycardia, atrioventricular block, fatigue, and masking of hypoglycaemic adrenergic symptoms in diabetes are commonly encountered. Abrupt cessation after chronic use can precipitate rebound hypertension and angina.

Acetaminophen, although among the safest analgesics in therapeutic doses, is responsible for a substantial fraction of acute liver failure cases in jurisdictions where high-dose products are widely available. Hepatotoxicity arises through NAPQI generation when glutathione stores are overwhelmed, with the threshold lowered in chronic alcohol use, fasting, and pre-existing liver disease. N-acetylcysteine is an effective antidote if administered within hours of ingestion. Inadvertent staggered overdose through combination products containing acetaminophen is a recognised cause of fatal poisoning.

Gadolinium deposition in the dentate nucleus and globus pallidus, demonstrated as increased signal on unenhanced imaging after repeated administration of linear gadolinium agents, has been documented even in patients with normal renal function. Although a clear clinical syndrome attributable to this retained gadolinium has not been established, the finding prompted regulatory restriction of several linear agents and a preference for macrocyclic alternatives in patients likely to need repeated imaging.

The absorption of levothyroxine is reduced by calcium and iron supplements, proton pump inhibitors, and certain foods, and a patient stabilised on a given dose can drift into hypothyroidism when one of these is introduced. Conversely, treating a malabsorptive condition can suddenly improve uptake and tip the patient into thyrotoxicosis, making interacting co-medications a recurring source of instability.

Drug withdrawals from market following post-marketing safety signals are uncommon but instructive. Cerivastatin was withdrawn in two thousand one after a disproportionate signal for rhabdomyolysis, particularly in combination with gemfibrozil. Cisapride was withdrawn in two thousand following recognition of fatal QT prolongation, particularly in patients with hepatic impairment or concurrent CYP3A4 inhibitors. Each withdrawal represents a regulatory judgement that the post-marketing risk-benefit balance has shifted unfavourably, often based on the recognition of off-label use, vulnerable subpopulations, or interactions not adequately characterised pre-approval.

H2-receptor antagonists are generally well tolerated, but the older cimetidine is a potent inhibitor of multiple CYP isoenzymes and produces clinically significant interactions with warfarin, phenytoin, and theophylline. Gynaecomastia and erectile dysfunction in men, through anti-androgenic effects on receptor binding, were reasons for cimetidine being supplanted by ranitidine and famotidine. Ranitidine was withdrawn from the global market in twenty-twenty after discovery of N-nitrosodimethylamine contamination that increased with shelf life and represented a probable carcinogen.

Postoperative nausea and vomiting remains one of the most common and distressing complications of general anaesthesia, with risk strongly predicted by female sex, non-smoking status, a history of motion sickness, and the use of volatile agents and perioperative opioids. Beyond patient discomfort, severe vomiting can disrupt surgical wounds, cause aspiration, and delay discharge, and multimodal antiemetic prophylaxis is now standard for high-risk patients.

Discontinuation of opioids after chronic use produces a withdrawal syndrome of yawning, lacrimation, rhinorrhoea, piloerection, abdominal cramping, and intense dysphoria, which, although rarely life-threatening in adults, is severe enough to drive resumption of use. In the neonate exposed in utero, the analogous neonatal abstinence syndrome can be life-threatening and requires structured pharmacologic management.

Promethazine and other first-generation antihistamines, formerly used freely as sedatives and antiemetics in young children, have been associated with respiratory depression and rarely death in children under two. Regulatory contraindications now apply. The risk of paradoxical excitation, hallucinations, and anticholinergic delirium in older children and adolescents is similarly underappreciated. Second-generation non-sedating antihistamines have largely supplanted these agents for allergic indications, although the absence of pleasant taste and easy-to-administer liquid formulations in some markets remains a practical issue.

Withdrawal from chronic glucocorticoid therapy can unmask a suppressed hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, producing an adrenal crisis with hypotension, hypoglycaemia, and shock if the dose is reduced too quickly or if an intercurrent illness increases steroid demand. The recovery of endogenous cortisol production after prolonged suppression may take months, mandating a slow taper and stress-dose cover.

Diuretics given to treat oedema can, through excessive volume depletion and neurohormonal activation, paradoxically promote sodium and water retention, a state of diuretic resistance and rebound that can make the underlying oedema harder to control. The compensatory physiology that the diuretic provokes works against its intended effect.

Pentamidine, used in Pneumocystis pneumonia in patients intolerant of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and in selected protozoal infections including leishmaniasis, has a difficult safety profile including pancreatitis, hyperglycaemia or hypoglycaemia through pancreatic islet cell toxicity, nephrotoxicity, and QT prolongation. Inhaled formulations for prophylaxis substantially reduce systemic toxicity but produce bronchospasm and have lower efficacy than systemic alternatives. Aerosolised use also raises the concern of unrecognised extrapulmonary Pneumocystis disease, a particular issue in the AIDS era that has receded with modern antiretroviral therapy.

Proton pump inhibitors are remarkably safe in short-term use but have accumulated a list of long-term association signals. Vitamin B12 deficiency, hypomagnesaemia, decreased calcium absorption with a small increase in hip fracture risk, an increased incidence of community-acquired pneumonia, and Clostridioides difficile colitis have all been demonstrated in observational data. The strength of the causal interpretation varies, and the benefit in patients with appropriate indications generally outweighs these risks, but de-escalation in patients without a clear ongoing indication is now recommended.

Negative pressure pulmonary oedema can develop within minutes of extubation when a patient generates strong inspiratory effort against an obstructed airway, most often from laryngospasm. The large negative intrathoracic pressure draws fluid into the alveoli, producing acute hypoxaemia and frothy secretions that may be mistaken for aspiration or cardiac failure, and prompt recognition is needed to guide appropriate respiratory support.

Intravenous lipid emulsions, particularly when infused rapidly, can produce fat overload syndrome with fever, hepatosplenomegaly, coagulopathy, and respiratory distress, reflecting an exceeded capacity to clear the lipid load. The condition is more common in neonates and in patients with impaired lipid metabolism, and it resolves on slowing or interrupting the lipid infusion.

Immune checkpoint inhibitors can provoke autoimmune endocrinopathies that are frequently permanent, including hypophysitis, thyroid dysfunction, primary adrenal insufficiency, and a fulminant insulin-dependent diabetes. Unlike many immune-related toxicities, these endocrine effects often do not resolve with immunosuppression, leaving the patient with a lifelong hormone deficiency that must be replaced.

Anticholinergic mydriatics used to facilitate fundus examination may precipitate acute angle-closure glaucoma in eyes with anatomically narrow anterior chamber angles. Although the absolute risk is low, the consequences of acute angle closure include irreversible visual loss if untreated within hours. Tropicamide is generally preferred over the longer-acting cyclopentolate or atropine where prolonged mydriasis is not required. Systemic anticholinergic effects from absorbed mydriatic drops can produce confusion in elderly patients.

The lipid nanoparticles that deliver messenger RNA vaccines function in part as adjuvants, and components such as polyethylene glycol within them have been implicated in the rare anaphylactic reactions observed shortly after these vaccines. The recognition that a delivery and adjuvant component, rather than the antigen, can drive immediate hypersensitivity has shaped post-vaccination observation protocols.

Off-label prescribing in paediatrics has historically been the norm because dedicated paediatric clinical trials were uncommon. Regulatory incentives in the European Union and the United States have substantially increased the proportion of medications with paediatric labelling, but information gaps persist particularly in neonatal populations, where pharmacokinetic complexity is greatest and clinical trial conduct is most challenging. The increased recognition of paediatric-specific adverse effect profiles, including effects on growth and neurodevelopment, has informed the regulatory push for proper paediatric study programmes.

Wrong-route errors are among the most catastrophic perioperative medication mistakes, and the inadvertent intrathecal administration of vincristine, intended for intravenous use, has been uniformly fatal. International measures to make such errors mechanically impossible, including dedicated connectors and minibag dilution, were adopted precisely because the consequence of the error admits no remedy.

Yohimbine, marketed as a supplement for sexual dysfunction and weight loss, is an alpha-2 adrenergic antagonist that can precipitate hypertensive crisis, tachyarrhythmia, and anxiety, particularly when combined with stimulants or monoamine oxidase inhibitors. Because the actual alkaloid content of marketed products varies enormously and is often unlabelled, the dose ingested is unpredictable, complicating both clinical use and toxicological assessment of adverse events.

subtopic: gene therapy and viral vector toxicity
sentence: Lentiviral vectors used to genetically modify cells for ex vivo gene therapy carry a theoretical risk of generating replication-competent virus and of insertional oncogenesis, and the manufactured cell products are tested extensively for these hazards before reinfusion. The complexity of the manufacturing introduces its own potential for product-related adverse events.

A paradoxical drug reaction is one in which a medication produces an effect opposite to its intended action, and a well-recognised example is the paradoxical bronchospasm that can follow inhalation of a beta-agonist bronchodilator. The patient who deteriorates after using a reliever inhaler illustrates how the expected pharmacology can, in a minority of individuals, reverse.

Drug-food interactions are sometimes underappreciated relative to drug-drug interactions. Grapefruit juice inhibits intestinal CYP3A4 and elevates exposure of substrates including statins, calcium-channel blockers, and several immunosuppressants. Tyramine-containing foods produce hypertensive crisis with monoamine oxidase inhibitors and have been the subject of long-standing dietary restrictions. Calcium-rich foods reduce absorption of quinolones and tetracyclines, and high-vitamin-K vegetables affect warfarin. The clinical task includes patient education appropriate to the specific drug regimen and the realistic dietary pattern of the patient.

Bleeding from antithrombotic therapy is not merely an acute event but a marker of worse long-term outcome, since a major bleed often prompts interruption of the antithrombotic drug, exposing the patient to a rebound thrombotic risk, and the bleed itself, through transfusion and inflammation, may independently worsen prognosis.

Calcium channel blockers and other vasodilating antihypertensives can produce reflex tachycardia and, in patients with coronary disease, a paradoxical worsening of angina, as the fall in blood pressure triggers a compensatory sympathetic surge. The undesired reflex response can offset or reverse the intended cardiovascular benefit.

Opioid prescribing has been recalibrated globally after recognition of substantial harms beyond respiratory depression. Tolerance develops differentially across opioid effects, with bowel motility least affected, producing the chronic constipation that limits long-term use. Opioid-induced hyperalgesia, a paradoxical sensitisation to pain with chronic high-dose therapy, complicates dose escalation in non-malignant pain. Hypogonadism with reduced libido, depression, and osteoporosis from chronic opioid use is increasingly recognised and contributes to the case for dose reduction.

Foscarnet, an antiviral used for resistant cytomegalovirus infection, chelates divalent cations and produces acute, sometimes symptomatic, falls in ionised calcium and magnesium during infusion, which can manifest as paraesthesiae, tetany, and arrhythmia. The electrolyte effect is tied directly to the rate of infusion.

Congenital long QT syndrome confers a latent vulnerability that may remain silent until a QT-prolonging drug unmasks it, producing syncope or sudden death. A family history of sudden cardiac death or unexplained syncope is therefore relevant to drug selection, and the recognition of drug-induced events sometimes leads to the diagnosis of an underlying inherited channelopathy in the patient or relatives.

Real-world evidence from electronic health records and administrative claims databases has become a major source of pharmacovigilance data, complementing spontaneous reporting and randomised trials. Self-controlled case series, propensity-score-matched cohort analyses, and active comparator new-user designs reduce confounding and provide effect estimates that may translate to clinical practice. The findings from these methods are increasingly accepted in regulatory decision-making, although the limitations of unmeasured confounding and the need for replication in independent data sources remain real constraints on causal inference.

Antithymocyte globulin, used for induction immunosuppression and treatment of acute rejection, produces a cytokine release reaction on first administration with fever, rigors, and hypotension, and serum sickness can follow as antibodies form against the heterologous protein. Profound and prolonged lymphocyte depletion leaves the recipient vulnerable to opportunistic viral and fungal infection for months afterward.

Sore throat, hoarseness, and dysphagia are frequent after tracheal intubation and reflect mucosal trauma, while a small minority of patients sustain more serious laryngeal injury including arytenoid dislocation or vocal cord paresis. Symptoms persisting beyond a few days warrant laryngoscopic evaluation, since unrecognised arytenoid dislocation becomes progressively harder to reduce as fibrosis sets in.

Renal or hepatic impairment can convert a normally safe QT-prolonging drug into a hazardous one by allowing the parent compound or an active metabolite to accumulate above the concentration at which channel blockade becomes clinically significant. Dose adjustment for organ function is therefore an integral part of safe prescribing for any drug with QT liability.

During the early response to the COVID-19 pandemic, the combination of hydroxychloroquine with azithromycin generated concern about additive QT prolongation, and several reports of torsades de pointes followed its widespread off-label use. The episode served as a real-time demonstration of how the rapid, large-scale deployment of QT-prolonging drugs can produce a measurable cardiac safety signal.

subtopic: gene therapy and viral vector toxicity
sentence: Systemic administration of viral vectors can trigger an acute innate immune response with cytokine release, complement activation, and an inflammatory syndrome that, in the earliest history of the field, contributed to a fatal outcome in a clinical trial. The event led to a fundamental rethinking of vector dosing and patient selection for gene therapy.

Succinylcholine, a depolarising neuromuscular blocker, transiently raises serum potassium, and in patients with burns, crush injury, denervation, or prolonged immobilisation this rise can be exaggerated to the point of cardiac arrest because of upregulated extrajunctional acetylcholine receptors. The drug is therefore avoided in these populations, and the hyperkalaemic hazard is one of the principal reasons for its restricted use.

Pioglitazone, the surviving thiazolidinedione after the withdrawal of rosiglitazone for cardiovascular reasons, lowers HbA1c through PPAR-gamma agonism but produces weight gain, fluid retention with congestive heart failure exacerbation, and an increased risk of distal limb fractures particularly in women. A signal for bladder cancer with longer-term use led to regulatory warnings and contraindication in patients with active bladder cancer or unexplained haematuria. The agent retains a niche in patients with marked insulin resistance and intact cardiac function.

Patients receiving renal replacement therapy present a complex dosing problem, since dialysis itself removes some drugs and not others, and the drug concentration achieved depends on the modality, the membrane, and the timing of doses relative to dialysis sessions. Both underdosing, with loss of efficacy, and accumulation between sessions, with toxicity, are real hazards in this population.

Tenfold dosing errors, arising from misplaced decimal points or from confusion between concentration and total dose, are particularly dangerous with potent agents such as opioids, adrenaline, and insulin, and they are disproportionately harmful in paediatric anaesthesia, where doses are calculated by weight. A single calculation slip can deliver a lethal quantity of drug.

Phenazopyridine, a urinary analgesic that turns the urine orange, can precipitate methaemoglobinaemia and haemolytic anaemia, particularly in patients with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency or when the drug accumulates in renal impairment. Prolonged use beyond the recommended few days risks these haematologic complications, and the staining of body fluids can interfere with laboratory assays and stain contact lenses permanently.

Vitamin K-rich herbal preparations and dietary changes can antagonise warfarin, producing a sub-therapeutic international normalised ratio and thrombotic risk, while other supplements potentiate the drug. Patients who self-medicate with green tea extracts, cranberry products, or various traditional remedies introduce a moving target into anticoagulant monitoring, and unexplained INR instability frequently traces to undisclosed supplement use.

Calcineurin inhibitors such as ciclosporin and tacrolimus produce nephrotoxicity through afferent arteriolar vasoconstriction, eventually progressing to interstitial fibrosis with prolonged exposure. Both agents are diabetogenic, with tacrolimus particularly associated with new-onset diabetes after transplantation. Ciclosporin produces hirsutism and gingival hyperplasia, while tacrolimus more often causes neurotoxicity manifesting as tremor, headache, and rarely posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome.

Numerous drugs raise serum prolactin by blocking dopaminergic inhibition of its secretion, with antipsychotics, metoclopramide, and some antidepressants being common culprits. The resulting hyperprolactinaemia produces galactorrhoea, menstrual disturbance, sexual dysfunction, and, over time, reduced bone density, and the laboratory finding is sometimes mistaken for a pituitary tumour before the medication history clarifies the cause.

Methadone used in opioid agonist maintenance prolongs the QT interval in a dose-dependent manner, and torsades de pointes has been documented at the higher doses sometimes required for adequate maintenance. Baseline and periodic electrocardiography is recommended, particularly with concurrent QT-prolonging agents or electrolyte disturbance, and the drug's long and variable half-life means that toxicity from accumulation can appear days after a dose increase.

Methotrexate pneumonitis is an idiosyncratic, potentially severe hypersensitivity reaction that can occur at the low doses used in rheumatology and is not predictable from the dose or duration of treatment. It presents with dyspnoea, dry cough, and fever, and because it can be life-threatening, any unexplained respiratory symptoms in a patient on methotrexate warrant prompt evaluation and consideration of drug cessation.

Hyperhidrosis is a common and underrecognised adverse effect of methadone maintenance, sometimes severe enough to disrupt sleep and daily functioning and to drive requests for dose reduction. The mechanism is thought to involve opioid effects on central thermoregulation, and the symptom can be difficult to manage without compromising the adequacy of the maintenance dose.

Tetracyclines including doxycycline produce permanent yellow-brown staining of developing teeth when administered to children under eight years and to mothers in the second and third trimesters of pregnancy, through binding to calcium ions in mineralising teeth. The drugs also impair bone growth temporarily. These effects led to the restriction of tetracycline use in young children that persists in current guidance, although the relatively brief courses used for serious infections such as rickettsial disease are now considered acceptable on individual risk-benefit grounds.

Heavy metal contamination of traditional remedies has produced clusters of lead, mercury, and arsenic poisoning, with certain Ayurvedic preparations deliberately incorporating metals as part of the formulation. Cases of severe lead encephalopathy in adults and developmental harm in children have been traced to such products, and the absence of regulatory premarket testing for many supplement categories leaves these exposures largely undetected until clinical poisoning occurs.

Reversal of anticoagulation in intracranial haemorrhage carries the particular hazard that aggressive procoagulant therapy may convert a survivable bleed into a fatal thrombotic stroke or systemic embolism, especially in patients with mechanical valves or recent venous thromboembolism. The clinician must weigh haematoma expansion against thrombotic catastrophe, and the optimal timing for reinstating anticoagulation after the bleed is stabilised remains an unresolved and high-stakes clinical dilemma.

The risk of torsades de pointes from a QT-prolonging drug is sharply amplified by hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, bradycardia, female sex, and the simultaneous use of more than one QT-prolonging agent. This means that a drug tolerated in isolation can become dangerous when a diuretic depletes potassium or a second QT-prolonging medication is added, and the cumulative effect must be assessed for the whole regimen.

Orthostatic hypotension is common in older adults and is exacerbated by a wide range of medications including antihypertensives, alpha-blockers used in benign prostatic hyperplasia, diuretics, tricyclic antidepressants, levodopa preparations, and the second-generation antipsychotics. Falls attributable to orthostatic hypotension produce a substantial fraction of hip fractures and intracranial haemorrhages in the elderly. Routine measurement of standing blood pressure after sitting, and gradual rather than abrupt dose escalation, are recommended preventive strategies. Compression stockings and judicious salt loading may complement medication adjustment in resistant cases.

Propofol produces dose-dependent hypotension and respiratory depression at induction and a characteristic injection-site pain that can be ameliorated by lidocaine pre-treatment. Prolonged high-dose infusion in critically ill patients may produce propofol infusion syndrome with metabolic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, hyperkalaemia, hepatic dysfunction, and cardiovascular collapse, particularly in children and in patients receiving concurrent vasopressors and corticosteroids. The syndrome was responsible for several fatal cases in paediatric intensive care during the early adoption of high-dose sedation regimens and has restricted current dosing.

CAR T-cell therapies have transformed outcomes for refractory B-cell malignancies but produce two characteristic toxicities. Cytokine release syndrome ranges from fever and hypotension to multiorgan failure, treated with the IL-6 receptor antagonist tocilizumab. Immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity, formerly called CRES, produces tremor, aphasia, and in severe cases seizures and cerebral oedema, and is graded with a dedicated assessment instrument.
